x.A: A Snowball Edge device transfers data offline by shipping. It isn't an online transfer, so this answer doesn't fit "online data transfer".
x.B: DataSync transfers data online from on premises to S3 and automatically verifies the integrity of the data after the transfer.
x.C: S3 File Gateway presents a file share and uploads to S3, but it doesn't run an integrity validation step for a one-time migration the way DataSync does.
x.D: Transfer Acceleration speeds up uploads over long distances, but it doesn't validate data integrity after the transfer, and it isn't something configured on premises.

x.A: Route 53 is a highly available, managed DNS service. Creating the hosted zones and importing the zone files moves the DNS to a managed service with no servers to run.
x.B: A single EC2 instance is a single point of failure, and you'd still manage the DNS server.
x.C: Migrating the servers as they are keeps the management burden and the single-server availability issues.
x.D: An Auto Scaling group with a desired capacity of 1 still means running and managing DNS software on EC2, and scaling on CPU doesn't suit DNS.

x.A: A Config rule isn't designed to report the count of incomplete multipart uploads across all buckets.
x.B: SCPs control permissions and can't report on S3 uploads.
x.C: S3 Storage Lens provides organization-wide metrics, including incomplete multipart upload bytes and object counts, across accounts and Regions in a dashboard, with no custom work.
x.D: A Multi-Region Access Point routes requests to buckets in several Regions and doesn't report on incomplete uploads.

x.A: A snapshot protects data, but upgrading the production instance in place means downtime and testing against live data, with a risk if the upgrade fails.
x.B: Native backup and restore to a new instance takes time and means downtime while data is moved.
x.C: DMS replication needs setup and ongoing management for the migration and cutover, which is more effort.
x.D: RDS Blue/Green Deployments create a synchronized staging copy of production where you upgrade and test, then switch over quickly with no data loss and little downtime.

x.A: An EC2 Reserved Instance bills 24 hours a day, but the job runs only 2 hours daily.
x.B: Lambda has a 15 minute limit, so a 2 hour job can't run.
x.C: Fargate runs the job as a task for up to as long as needed, and you pay only for the 2 hours of compute each day. EventBridge schedules it, with no servers to manage.
x.D: ECS on EC2 needs an EC2 instance, which bills while it runs and requires management.

x.A: Neptune is the right graph database, but Kinesis Data Streams would be extra setup because Neptune has a built-in change stream.
x.B: Neptune is a graph database that suits relationships and recommendations, and Neptune Streams captures every change to the graph with no extra components, so it needs the least operational overhead.
x.C: QLDB is a ledger database for immutable transaction records, not for analyzing relationships between entities.
x.D: QLDB isn't a graph database, and Neptune Streams only works with Neptune.

x.A: Glacier is archive storage with retrieval delays, so it can't support hourly analysis and modification by instances.
x.B: An EBS volume attaches to a single instance in one AZ, so several instances across AZs can't share it, and its size is limited.
x.C: EFS is a shared file system that Linux instances across multiple AZs can mount simultaneously, and it grows automatically as the data grows.
x.D: A Provisioned IOPS EBS volume can be shared only within a single AZ with Multi-Attach, and not across multiple AZs.

x.A: The standby in a Multi-AZ deployment can't serve read traffic, because it's only for failover.
x.B: Transfer Acceleration is an S3 feature and doesn't apply to RDS.
x.C: A read replica gets a copy of the data, and sending read queries to it takes load off the primary database, which improves performance.
x.D: Firehose delivers streaming data to destinations like S3, and doesn't increase concurrency of requests to RDS.

x.A: S3 doesn't have global tables, which is a DynamoDB feature, and replicating the data for each agency would be costly.
x.B: Making the bucket public exposes the telemetry data to everyone, which isn't secure.
x.C: Cross-account access with a bucket policy (or access points) gives each agency's account read access to the existing bucket, which is secure and needs no copies.
x.D: Creating an IAM user for each analyst in the source account doesn't scale and gives the agencies' people long-term credentials in the company's account.

x.A: Copying the data to S3 with a Lambda function means building and running a custom job, and S3 doesn't offer the same CIFS and NFS protocols.
x.B: Restoring from an AWS Backup copy requires creating a new file system from the backup during a disaster, which is slower and more manual.
x.C: An FSx for ONTAP file system in the secondary Region with NetApp SnapMirror replicates the data natively, so the DR Region supports the same CIFS and NFS protocols, with the least operational overhead.
x.D: EFS supports NFS only, not CIFS, and migrating the data off ONTAP is a big change.

x.A: Processing the event in ECS before Lambda adds a container service to run and doesn't buffer the events.
x.B: Processing the event in EKS adds a Kubernetes cluster to run and doesn't buffer the events.
x.C: An SNS subscription that delivers to an SQS queue buffers the events, and the queue triggers the Lambda function, so it scales with the number of events and doesn't lose events.
x.D: AWS SMS (Server Migration Service) is a migration service and isn't an event target.

x.A: Fargate runs containers continuously, and scaling from 0 to 500 requests per second isn't as instant or as cost-effective for unpredictable traffic.
x.B: Lambda scales automatically from zero to hundreds of requests per second and you pay only for the requests, which suits unpredictable traffic behind API Gateway.
x.C: DynamoDB is a key-value database that scales with unpredictable growth and traffic, and fits simple key-value queries.
x.D: EC2 Auto Scaling adds capacity slowly and keeps paying for instances when there are no requests.
x.E: Aurora is relational and costs more than needed for simple key-value data under 1 GB.

x.A: A Lambda function can generate S3 presigned URLs that give employees temporary access to upload or download specific data. It's secure and needs very little to manage.
x.B: An IAM user and policy for every employee around the world is a lot to manage and uses long-term credentials.
x.C: A File Gateway is for on-premises file access, and having employees mount shares from their own computers around the world adds operations.
x.D: Transfer Family SFTP with a custom identity provider and Secrets Manager means building and maintaining the authentication for the users.

x.A: Sticky sessions keep a client on the same instance, so some instances receive more traffic than others. Disabling them lets the ALB spread requests evenly.
x.B: An NLB would balance connections but doesn't address the uneven distribution caused by session stickiness, and it loses ALB features.
x.C: More instances don't fix an uneven distribution, because sticky clients still stick to one instance.
x.D: Health check frequency affects how quickly unhealthy instances are detected, not how traffic is distributed.

x.A: A Lambda resource policy controls who can invoke the function, and kms:Decrypt isn't granted there.
x.B: The KMS key policy must allow the Lambda function's IAM role to use the key to decrypt, because KMS requires access to be allowed in the key policy.
x.C: A resource policy of the Lambda function isn't a principal in the KMS key policy. The execution role is.
x.D: IAM policies attach to roles, users, or groups, not directly to a Lambda function.
x.E: The Lambda function's execution role needs the kms:Decrypt permission so it can decrypt the files it downloads.

x.A: Delivering reports to Kinesis isn't a supported path for Cost and Usage Reports, and EMR is costly for a monthly query.
x.B: Cost and Usage Reports enabled in the management account cover all member accounts, S3 is the delivery target, and Athena queries the data with SQL only when you run it, so it's scalable and cost-effective.
x.C: Reports are enabled from the management account, not per member account, and Redshift is more costly than Athena for monthly queries.
x.D: Cost and Usage Reports can't be delivered to Kinesis, and enabling them per member account isn't needed.

x.A: A Network Load Balancer supports UDP and distributes traffic across the Auto Scaling group's instances, which scale out and in with the traffic.
x.B: An ALB supports HTTP and HTTPS only, so it can't carry UDP traffic.
x.C: Weighted DNS routing doesn't scale with health or load the way a load balancer does, and it isn't connected to the Auto Scaling group.
x.D: A NAT instance with port forwarding is a single point of failure and doesn't scale.

x.A: Storing logs in S3 is cheap, and Athena queries them with standard SQL only when run, so it's cost-effective for weekly on-demand analysis.
x.B: RDS runs and bills continuously and doesn't scale well for tens of gigabytes of logs per day.
x.C: An OpenSearch Service cluster runs all the time, which costs more for weekly queries, and it doesn't use standard SQL by default.
x.D: An EMR cluster running continuously costs more, and it needs management.

x.A: A public ACM certificate for the apex domain and a wildcard for *.example.com covers example.com and every country subdomain on the ALB, with no per-subdomain certificates.
x.B: A private certificate isn't trusted by browsers for a public website.
x.C: A single public and private certificate for the apex domain doesn't cover the subdomains.
x.D: Email validation is manual and doesn't support automatic renewal. DNS validation is the better method, and switching isn't what's asked.
x.E: Validating ownership with DNS records is automatic, and supports renewal of the certificates with no manual steps.

x.A: A CloudHSM key store keeps keys in AWS-managed HSMs in your account (within AWS), not in an on-premises key manager, so keys don't stay outside AWS.
x.B: A KMS external key store (XKS) lets KMS use keys that are held in an external key manager outside AWS, from various vendors, so keys remain on premises.
x.C: The default KMS key store keeps key material in AWS, which doesn't meet the requirement.
x.D: A custom key store backed by CloudHSM keeps keys in AWS, not outside, and it adds the work of operating the cluster.

x.A: EFS offers latencies in the low milliseconds, not within 1 ms, so it doesn't meet the latency requirement for HPC.
x.B: S3 can't be mounted as a POSIX shared file system with sub-millisecond latency for parallel HPC processing.
x.C: FSx for Lustre provides sub-millisecond latency and high throughput for parallel access from hundreds of instances, and it links to an S3 bucket so engineers can access the results afterward.
x.D: RAM doesn't let you mount an S3 bucket as a file system on instances.

x.A: Global Accelerator provides static anycast IP addresses and routes users to the nearest healthy endpoint, with automatic failover across Regions that doesn't depend on DNS caching on devices. It supports UDP for VoIP.
x.B: Route 53 routing depends on DNS, and devices may cache IP addresses, so failover isn't immediate. Geolocation also isn't based on lowest latency.
x.C: CloudFront doesn't support UDP, so it can't carry VoIP traffic.
x.D: An ALB works in a single Region and doesn't support UDP or cross-Region failover.

x.A: Scratch file systems are for temporary data and aren't replicated, so they aren't highly available.
x.B: Persistent FSx for Lustre file systems are highly available and replicate data within an AZ, support sustained throughput, sub-millisecond latency, and access by thousands of instances at once.
x.C: EFS with Bursting Throughput provides latency in the low milliseconds and its throughput depends on the size, so it can't give sustained high throughput for thousands of instances.
x.D: EFS with Provisioned Throughput helps throughput, but its latency isn't sub-millisecond like Lustre.

x.A: gp2 ties IOPS to volume size, so you can't provision IOPS independent of capacity.
x.B: io1 lets you provision IOPS separately, but it costs more than gp3 for 15,000 IOPS.
x.C: gp3 lets you provision IOPS (up to 16,000) independently of storage size, and costs less than gp2 or io1 for this requirement.
x.D: Magnetic storage provides very low IOPS and can't reach 15,000.

x.A: RDS for SQL Server is a managed service, and read replicas serve reporting without affecting the production database, so it needs the least operational work.
x.B: SQL Server on EC2 means managing the operating system, patching, and Always On clustering yourself.
x.C: DynamoDB isn't SQL Server compatible, so the application and reports would be rewritten.
x.D: Aurora MySQL is a different engine, so migrating SQL Server to it needs schema and code conversion.
